content.intro: This lesson introduces post-installation maintenance as part of linux installation and environment setup. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Choose and prepare an appropriate practice environment while protecting existing data and verifying installation media.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks.

items.title: Applying system updates
items.text: Applying system updates: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.title: Installing essential utilities
items.text: Installing essential utilities: Use the tool appropriate to the distribution, inspect proposed changes first, and note the package/runtime version that determines behavior.

items.title: Enabling automatic security updates where appropriate
items.text: Enabling automatic security updates where appropriate: Check the effective identity and policy, prefer the minimum required privileges, and verify both allowed and denied access in a test environment.

items.title: Creating a recovery point or VM snapshot
items.text: Creating a recovery point or VM snapshot: A backup or rollback is useful only when its integrity and restoration procedure have been verified in a separate test location.

content_blocks.code: printf 'review updates -> apply in a maintenance window -> verify services -> record versions\n'
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Post-Installation Maintenance. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume post-installation maintenance behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: Planning output only; do not partition or install on a machine with important data for this exercise. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate post-installation maintenance. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Use a reversible practice setup first. Confirm hardware compatibility, installation media integrity, and a recovery path before changing disks.
